1.summary: In the Persian palace at Susa, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's wall is still broken down, and he mourns, fasts and prays for many days.
1.lookfor: Notice what Nehemiah does before he does anything else, how his prayer draws on older Scripture, and the job he mentions only in the very last line.

names.name: Nehemiah
names.gloss: A Jew serving at the Persian court, whose name means "Yahweh comforts."

names.name: Hacaliah
names.gloss: Nehemiah's father, known only from this book.

names.name: Shushan
names.gloss: Susa, in south-west Iran, a royal capital of the Persian kings and the setting of Esther.

names.name: Hanani
names.gloss: Nehemiah's brother or close relative, who brings news from Judah.

insights.title: Why the wall still lay broken
insights.body: Babylon had torn down Jerusalem's walls in 586 BC. The Temple had been rebuilt by 515 BC, but an attempt to rebuild the walls had been stopped by royal order, as Ezra records. A city without walls was open to raids and to contempt.

insights.title: A prayer woven from Scripture
insights.body: Nehemiah addresses "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness" (1:5), words close to Deuteronomy and to Daniel's prayer. His plea that God would gather the scattered even from "the uttermost part of the heavens" (1:9) rests on a promise in Deuteronomy.

insights.title: I and my father's house
insights.body: Nehemiah confesses not only Israel's sins but "I and my father's house have sinned" (1:6). Living comfortably in the palace, he still counts himself among the guilty. Ezra and Daniel pray the same way.

insights.title: Cupbearer to the king
insights.body: Only the final line reveals that Nehemiah "was cup bearer to the king" (1:11). A royal cupbearer served and guarded the king's wine against poison and often became a trusted adviser. Joseph's story features Pharaoh's chief cupbearer.

insights.title: This man
insights.body: Nehemiah asks for mercy "in the sight of this man" (1:11). Before God, the most powerful king on earth is simply this man. The phrase captures the book's view that emperors act under God's hand.

insights.title: Exiles who stayed
insights.body: Nearly a century after Cyrus allowed the return, many Jews still lived across the Persian Empire, some in high positions, like Daniel, Esther and Mordecai. Nehemiah shows how such a person could use his position for the people in Judah.

insights.title: Months of waiting prayer
insights.body: Nehemiah heard the news in Chislev and spoke to the king in Nisan, about four months later. What would it look like to carry a burden in prayer that long before acting?

2.summary: The king notices Nehemiah's sadness and grants his request to go and rebuild Jerusalem; Nehemiah inspects the walls by night and rallies the people, despite mockery from local leaders.
2.lookfor: Watch for the quick prayer in the middle of a conversation, the letters and timber he asks for, his secret night ride, and the three men who oppose him.

names.name: Artaxerxes
names.gloss: Artaxerxes I, king of Persia from 465 to 424 BC.

names.name: Asaph
names.gloss: Keeper of the king's forest, a royal official in charge of timber; not the singer of David's day.

names.name: Sanballat the Horonite
names.gloss: Governor of Samaria, probably from Beth Horon; his name is Babylonian.

names.name: Tobiah
names.gloss: An Ammonite official, probably in charge of the region east of the Jordan, with ties to Jerusalem's leading families.

names.name: Geshem the Arabian
names.gloss: A powerful Arab ruler to the south.

names.name: valley gate
names.gloss: A gate on the west side of the old city, facing the Tyropoeon Valley.

insights.title: A sad face before the king
insights.body: Courtiers were expected to look cheerful before the king, and Nehemiah "was very much afraid" when his sadness was noticed (2:2). The king's question gave him his opening. He speaks of the city as "the place of my fathers' tombs" (2:3), an appeal any ancient ruler would honour.

insights.title: Arrow prayer
insights.body: When the king asks what he wants, Nehemiah "prayed to the God of heaven" and then answered (2:4-5). The prayer must have been silent and brief, but it followed four months of prayer and fasting.

insights.title: Escort and the good hand
insights.body: Nehemiah credits his success to "the good hand of my God on me" (2:8), the same phrase used of Ezra. Unlike Ezra, who refused a guard, Nehemiah travels with army officers and horsemen (2:9). Both are presented as faithful.

insights.title: Sanballat and Geshem outside the Bible
insights.body: Papyri from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt, written around 407 BC, name Sanballat as governor of Samaria and mention his sons. A silver bowl from Egypt names Gashmu, king of Qedar, an Arab kingdom, who many scholars identify with Geshem.

insights.title: Why the neighbours objected
insights.body: A walled Jerusalem would become a rival centre of power to Samaria and a threat to others' influence. The opponents frame it as rebellion against the king (2:19), the same charge that had stopped the earlier work.

insights.title: No portion, right or memorial
insights.body: Nehemiah tells his opponents they have "no portion, nor right, nor memorial, in Jerusalem" (2:20). The three terms cover property, legal claim and a place in the city's memory or worship. The line echoes Zerubbabel's answer to an earlier offer of help.

insights.title: Building with God
insights.body: The people answer, "Let's rise up and build" (2:18), and Nehemiah tells his opponents "The God of heaven will prosper us" (2:20). Planning, permits and timber all matter in this book, but so does dependence on God. The psalm says unless Yahweh builds the house, the builders labour in vain.

3.summary: A list of who rebuilt each section of Jerusalem's wall and gates, moving round the city from the sheep gate back to the sheep gate.
3.lookfor: Look for the high priest at the start, the people who built near their own homes, the nobles who would not work, and the daughters who did.

names.name: Eliashib the high priest
names.gloss: Grandson of Jeshua, the high priest of the first return.

names.name: sheep gate
names.gloss: A gate in the north wall near the Temple, where animals for sacrifice may have been brought in.

names.name: Tekoites
names.gloss: People of Tekoa, a town south of Bethlehem and the prophet Amos's home.

names.name: Shallum the son of Hallohesh
names.gloss: A district ruler who built with his daughters.

names.name: dung gate
names.gloss: A gate at the southern end of the city, leading to the Hinnom Valley where refuse was dumped.

names.name: Ophel
names.gloss: The hill between the City of David and the Temple Mount.

names.name: Beth Zur
names.gloss: A town in the hills south of Jerusalem.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter is a list of builders and wall sections. Skim the names, but read who starts the work, the Tekoite nobles, Shallum's daughters, and the people working opposite their own houses.

insights.title: Why list every builder
insights.body: Ancient building inscriptions honoured the people who paid for or carried out work. This record does the same, giving each family credit for a section. It also shows the whole community, priests, rulers, craftsmen and towns, sharing the work.

insights.title: Starting with the priests
insights.body: The high priest and his fellow priests build the sheep gate first and consecrate it (3:1). The wall around the Temple area comes first, and holiness frames the whole project. Yet later Eliashib makes room in the Temple for Nehemiah's enemy Tobiah.

insights.title: Nobles who would not stoop
insights.body: The Tekoites built, "but their nobles didn't put their necks to the Lord's work" (3:5). The phrase pictures oxen refusing the yoke. The ordinary Tekoites went on to repair a second section as well (3:27).

insights.title: Building in front of your own house
insights.body: Several people repair the wall opposite their own houses (3:10, 3:23, 3:28-30). This was practical, since they lived there, and it gave them a strong reason to build well. Their own families would depend on that stretch of wall.

insights.title: He and his daughters
insights.body: Shallum, a district ruler, built "he and his daughters" (3:12). The note is unusual in a list of men. Some suggest he had no sons; either way, the daughters' work was remembered.

insights.title: The sheep gate in John
insights.body: The list begins and ends at the sheep gate (3:1, 3:32). Centuries later John places the pool of Bethesda, where Jesus heals a lame man, "by the sheep gate." The gate stood near the Temple's north side.

insights.title: Tracing the wall today
insights.body: The circuit can be partly traced, from the sheep gate in the north, west to the valley gate, south to the dung and spring gates and up the east side. Archaeologists have uncovered sections of wall in the City of David that some date to Nehemiah's time, though the dating is debated.

insights.title: Repairers of the breach
insights.body: Isaiah promised that God's people would rebuild ancient ruins and be called Repairer of the Breach. Nehemiah 3 is that promise in practical form: ordinary people repairing one section at a time.

4.summary: Opponents mock and then plot to attack the builders, so Nehemiah sets guards and arms the workers, who build with a weapon in one hand.
4.lookfor: Notice how the opposition grows from jokes to threats, how Nehemiah combines prayer and practical defence, and what the workers carry.

names.name: Sanballat
names.gloss: Governor of Samaria and Nehemiah's main opponent.

names.name: Tobiah the Ammonite
names.gloss: Sanballat's ally from east of the Jordan.

names.name: Ashdodites
names.gloss: People of Ashdod, the old Philistine city on the coast west of Jerusalem.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: The Persian province north of Judah, governed by Sanballat.

insights.title: If a fox climbed it
insights.body: Tobiah jokes that even a fox would break down their stone wall (4:3). Sanballat's taunts ask whether the "feeble Jews" can bring burned stones back to life (4:2). Fire weakens limestone and makes it crumble, so the jibe had some truth to it.

insights.title: A prayer for justice
insights.body: Nehemiah asks God not to cover his enemies' iniquity (4:4-5). Like the imprecatory psalms, it hands vengeance to God instead of taking it himself. Readers have long wrestled with such prayers alongside Jesus' command to pray for enemies.

insights.title: A mind to work
insights.body: The wall reached half its height "for the people had a mind to work" (4:6). The Hebrew is literally that the people had a heart to work. The next setback comes from inside: Judah complains the carriers are worn out and the rubble endless (4:10).

insights.title: Building with one hand
insights.body: The labourers "with one of his hands did the work, and with the other held his weapon" (4:17). Builders wore swords, half the men stood guard, and a trumpeter stayed by Nehemiah to call everyone to any point attacked (4:18-20). No one even took off their clothes at night (4:23).

insights.title: Remember the Lord
insights.body: Nehemiah urges, "Don't be afraid of them! Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome" (4:14). Moses had told Israel not to fear the nations, for Yahweh was among them, "a great and awesome God."

insights.title: Our God will fight for us
insights.body: Nehemiah's rallying cry is "Our God will fight for us" (4:20). The words recall Moses at the Red Sea and Joshua in the conquest, when Yahweh fought for Israel. Yet here God's fighting goes together with guards, weapons and planning.

insights.title: Prayer and a guard
insights.body: "We made our prayer to our God, and set a watch" (4:9). How do you hold together trusting God and taking sensible precautions?

5.summary: Poor Jews cry out that famine, taxes and debts are forcing them to sell their land and children, and Nehemiah makes the wealthy cancel the loans while refusing his own governor's allowance.
5.lookfor: Look for who is exploiting whom, what Nehemiah asks the lenders to give back, the gesture with his robe, and how he pays for his own table.

names.name: Artaxerxes
names.gloss: The Persian king whose tribute burdened the people.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: The small Persian province around Jerusalem.

insights.title: A crisis from within
insights.body: This crisis comes not from enemies but from fellow Jews. Famine, the king's tribute and debts meant families mortgaged fields and handed children over as debt-slaves (5:3-5). Work on the wall may have kept men from their fields and made things worse.

insights.title: The law on lending
insights.body: The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite and limited debt slavery. Nehemiah calls the lenders' practice "not good" (5:9) and asks them to give up the interest and return the land (5:11).

insights.title: Usury
insights.body: The Hebrew word massa here means a loan or a claim on a debtor, and the charge in 5:11 is "the hundredth part," probably one percent a month. That is twelve percent a year, modest by ancient standards, but the law forbade any interest to the poor.

insights.title: Shaking out the robe
insights.body: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his robe, used like a pocket, and says God should shake out anyone who breaks the promise (5:13). Paul later shook out his clothing as a sign that he was clear of responsibility.

insights.title: Refusing the governor's bread
insights.body: For twelve years Nehemiah did not take the food allowance governors were entitled to (5:14-15), yet fed 150 officials daily and guests besides (5:17-18). Paul similarly gave up his right to support so as not to burden the churches.

insights.title: Remember me
insights.body: The chapter ends with Nehemiah's first "Remember to me, my God, for good" (5:19). The prayer returns several times and closes the book. Some readers find it self-regarding; others see an honest appeal to God rather than people as judge.

insights.title: Justice as part of rebuilding
insights.body: A city with strong walls but exploited people would not be the community God wanted. The prophets of the time also condemned oppression of the poor. Rebuilding Jerusalem meant rebuilding justice as well.

6.summary: Nehemiah's enemies try a trap, a slander and a false prophecy to stop him, but the wall is finished in fifty-two days.
6.lookfor: Watch for the four invitations, the letter left open, the offer of safety in the Temple, and the speed of the finish.

names.name: Ono
names.gloss: A plain near the coast, far from Jerusalem and close to the opponents' territory.

names.name: Gashmu
names.gloss: Another form of the name Geshem.

names.name: Shemaiah the son of Delaiah
names.gloss: A prophet hired to frighten Nehemiah.

names.name: Noadiah
names.gloss: A prophetess who joined in trying to intimidate Nehemiah.

insights.title: A great work
insights.body: Invited four times to a meeting at Ono, Nehemiah answers, "I am doing a great work, so that I can't come down" (6:3). Ono was a long journey from Jerusalem and near his enemies' territory. Refusing kept both the work and his life safe.

insights.title: An open letter
insights.body: The fifth message is an "open letter" (6:5). Official letters were sealed, so an unsealed one was meant to be read along the way. It spread the rumour that Nehemiah planned to make himself king, a charge that could ruin him at court.

insights.title: Why not hide in the Temple?
insights.body: Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to shut himself inside the Temple (6:10). As a layman Nehemiah was forbidden to enter the sanctuary, which was reserved for priests. Had he fled there, he would have broken the law and looked like a coward (6:13).

insights.title: False prophets
insights.body: Nehemiah realises "God had not sent him" (6:12). Jeremiah had faced prophets who spoke comforting words God had not given them. Noadiah is one of a handful of women in the Bible called prophetess, alongside Miriam, Deborah and Huldah.

insights.title: Strengthen my hands
insights.body: Enemies hope the builders' "hands will be weakened" (6:9), and Nehemiah prays, "strengthen my hands." Weak hands mean lost courage and strong hands mean resolve, a picture found throughout Ezra and Nehemiah.

insights.title: Fifty-two days
insights.body: The wall was finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days (6:15). The speed suggests much of the old foundation could be reused. The historian Josephus later gives a period of over two years, perhaps including later work.

insights.title: Done by our God
insights.body: The nations lost their confidence, "for they perceived that this work was done by our God" (6:16). Even enemies could see God's hand in it. Yet the chapter ends with Tobiah still writing letters through his allies in Judah (6:17-19).

7.summary: With the wall finished, Nehemiah sets guards and finds that the city has few residents, so he consults the register of the first returnees, which is copied out in full.
7.lookfor: Notice the rules for the gates, the empty city, and how closely the list matches the one in Ezra 2.

names.name: Hanani
names.gloss: Nehemiah's brother, now put in charge of Jerusalem.

names.name: Hananiah the governor of the fortress
names.gloss: Commander of the citadel near the Temple, praised as faithful.

names.name: Zerubbabel
names.gloss: Leader of the first return under Cyrus, nearly a century earlier.

skim.advice: Verses 6 to 73 repeat the list of returnees from Ezra 2. Skim the families and numbers, but read verses 1 to 5 on securing and repopulating the city.

insights.title: Not until the sun is hot
insights.body: The gates are not to open "until the sun is hot" (7:3), well after dawn, when everyone is awake and alert. Residents guard the wall near their own houses, as many had built it near their houses.

insights.title: A large, empty city
insights.body: "The city was wide and large; but the people were few" (7:4). Walls are useless without people to defend and live within them. The problem is solved in chapter 11 when a tenth of the people move into the city.

insights.title: Ezra 2 again
insights.body: Nehemiah finds the register of the first return and copies it (7:5). It matches Ezra 2 closely, with small differences in names and numbers typical of copied lists. The same total, 42,360, appears in both.

insights.title: The book of the genealogy
insights.body: Family registers decided who could own land, serve as priests and belong to the community. Priests who could not show their descent were set aside (7:64), an issue that mattered for keeping the priesthood legitimate.

insights.title: Put into my heart
insights.body: Nehemiah says, "My God put into my heart to gather" the people (7:5). He uses the same words for his first plan to rebuild (2:12). He attributes his practical plans to God's prompting.

insights.title: Walls for a people
insights.body: The book turns here from the walls to the people inside them. The list sets up the reading of the law, the confession and the covenant in chapters 8 to 10. Jerusalem's restoration is about a people more than about stones.

8.summary: Ezra reads the law of Moses to the assembled people, the Levites explain it, the people weep and are told to celebrate, and they keep the feast of booths with great joy.
8.lookfor: Notice who asks for the book, how long the reading lasts, how the people respond when the book is opened, and why they are told not to weep.

names.name: Ezra the scribe
names.gloss: The priest and teacher of the law who came to Jerusalem some years before Nehemiah.

names.name: water gate
names.gloss: A gate on the east side of the city above the Gihon spring.

names.name: Levites
names.gloss: Members of the tribe of Levi who assisted the priests and taught the law.

names.name: Jeshua the son of Nun
names.gloss: Joshua, Moses' successor; Jeshua is a later form of the name.

names.name: Ephraim’s gate
names.gloss: A gate in the north wall, on the road toward the territory of Ephraim.

insights.title: The people asked for it
insights.body: The people gathered "as one man" and asked Ezra to bring the book (8:1). Men, women and all who could understand stood listening from early morning until midday (8:3). When Ezra opened the scroll, everyone stood up (8:5), a custom still kept in many synagogues and churches for the reading of Scripture.

insights.title: Gave the sense
insights.body: The Levites read "distinctly" and "gave the sense" (8:8). The Hebrew may mean they translated or explained, since many returnees spoke Aramaic rather than Hebrew. The Talmud sees here the beginning of the Targum, the Aramaic translations read alongside the Hebrew in synagogues.

insights.title: A wooden platform
insights.body: Ezra stood on "a pulpit of wood" (8:4), literally a wooden tower, built for the occasion, with leaders on either side. It is an early picture of public reading from a raised platform, which later became the bimah of the synagogue.

insights.title: Why they wept
insights.body: The people wept as they heard the law (8:9), probably realising how far they had fallen short of it. Nehemiah and Ezra told them the day was holy to God and a time for feasting, not mourning. The first day of the seventh month was a festival day.

insights.title: The joy of Yahweh
insights.body: "Don't be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength" (8:10). The joy may be the joy God gives or God's own delight in his people. Either way, the feast includes sending portions to those with nothing prepared, a custom Esther also records for Purim.

insights.title: Reading the law at the feast
insights.body: Moses had commanded the law to be read to all Israel, men, women, children and foreigners, at the feast of tents. The people discover the command about booths and keep it (8:14-17), with Ezra reading every day (8:18).

insights.title: Not since Joshua
insights.body: The writer says Israel had not kept the feast this way "since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun" (8:17). The returnees had kept the feast before, so the point is probably the scale and manner: everyone living in booths across the city.

insights.title: A people of the book
insights.body: This scene of Scripture read aloud, explained and obeyed by a whole community is often seen as a turning point. Israel was becoming a people shaped by a written text, a pattern later followed in synagogue and church alike.

9.summary: Gathered in sackcloth, the people read the law and confess their sins, and the Levites lead a long prayer reviewing Israel's history of rebellion and God's mercy.
9.lookfor: Trace the prayer through creation, Abraham, the exodus, the wilderness, the land, and the exile, and notice the recurring word "but" and how the prayer ends.

names.name: Abram
names.gloss: Abraham's original name, before God renamed him.

names.name: Ur of the Chaldees
names.gloss: An ancient city in southern Mesopotamia, Abraham's first home.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: An Amorite king east of the Jordan defeated by Israel under Moses.

names.name: Og king of Bashan
names.gloss: A king east of the Jordan defeated by Israel under Moses.

names.name: Kadmiel
names.gloss: Head of a Levite family who helps lead the prayer.

insights.title: Israel's story in one prayer
insights.body: This is the Bible's longest prayer, retelling the story from creation (9:6) through Abraham, the exodus, Sinai, the wilderness, the conquest, the judges, the prophets and the exile. Psalms 105 and 106 and Stephen's speech in Acts retell the same story in similar ways.

insights.title: A God ready to pardon
insights.body: The heart of the prayer calls God "gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness" (9:17). These words come from God's own self-description to Moses after the golden calf, and they echo across the Old Testament.

insights.title: Live in them
insights.body: The prayer cites the law "which if a man does, he shall live in them" (9:29), from Leviticus. Paul quotes the same verse twice in contrasting law and faith, a passage that Jewish and Christian readers interpret differently.

insights.title: Your good Spirit
insights.body: The prayer says God gave "your good Spirit to instruct them" in the wilderness (9:20) and warned them "by your Spirit through your prophets" (9:30). The Spirit appears here as the one who teaches and speaks through the prophets.

insights.title: Stiffened their neck
insights.body: Again and again the fathers "hardened their neck" (9:16-17, 9:29). The picture is an ox refusing to bend to the yoke. Stephen uses the same image when he calls his hearers stiff-necked.

insights.title: Servants in our own land
insights.body: The prayer ends, "we are servants today" in the very land God gave to their fathers (9:36). The harvest goes to the Persian kings (9:37). Even after the return, the community feels it is still in a kind of exile.

insights.title: Sackcloth and dirt
insights.body: The people come "with fasting, with sackcloth, and dirt on them" (9:1). Sackcloth was rough goat-hair cloth, and dust on the head was a sign of mourning. These outward signs went together with confession and reading of the law (9:3).

insights.title: Honest history
insights.body: The prayer tells Israel's story with all its failures, set against God's faithfulness. What might change if you told your own story that way?

10.summary: Leaders seal a written covenant, and the people swear to keep God's law, especially on marriage, the Sabbath, the seventh year and support for the Temple.
10.lookfor: Notice who signs first, the specific promises the people make, and the promise that closes the chapter.

names.name: Nehemiah the governor
names.gloss: The first to put his name to the covenant.

names.name: Levites
names.gloss: Temple assistants who received the people's tithes.

names.name: temple servants
names.gloss: Assistants in the Temple's work, below the Levites.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 27 list those who sealed the covenant. Skim the names, then read verses 28 to 39 closely for the commitments themselves.

insights.title: Putting promises in writing
insights.body: The covenant follows directly from the prayer in chapter 9, which ends, "we make a sure covenant, and write it" (9:38). Having confessed their history, the people commit to specific changes. Written and sealed agreements were normal in Persian legal life.

insights.title: A covenant with details
insights.body: The commitments are specific: no mixed marriages (10:30), no buying on the Sabbath (10:31), observing the seventh year and cancelling debts (10:31), and supporting the Temple (10:32-39). Several of them address the very problems Nehemiah later has to deal with again in chapter 13.

insights.title: The Temple tax
insights.body: The people pledge a third of a shekel a year for the Temple (10:32). The law of Moses spoke of half a shekel at a census. By Jesus' time the annual Temple tax was a half shekel, the two-drachma coin collected from Peter.

insights.title: The wood offering
insights.body: Families draw lots to bring wood for the altar at set times (10:34). The altar fire had to burn continually, and wood was scarce in the hills around Jerusalem. Josephus later mentions a festival of wood-bringing.

insights.title: A curse and an oath
insights.body: The people "entered into a curse, and into an oath" (10:29). Ancient covenants included curses that the oath-taker called on himself if he broke his word. Deuteronomy ends with such blessings and curses.

insights.title: Do not forsake the house
insights.body: The chapter closes, "We will not forsake the house of our God" (10:39). Later, Nehemiah returns to find the Levites unpaid and asks, "Why is God's house forsaken?" The prophet Malachi also rebukes the people for withholding tithes.

insights.title: Making faith concrete
insights.body: The people turned their repentance into specific promises about money, time and relationships. What concrete commitments would express your faith right now?

11.summary: One in ten of the people is chosen to live in Jerusalem, and the chapter lists the families who settled there and the towns where the rest lived.
11.lookfor: Notice how residents are chosen, the people who volunteer, and how far the list of towns stretches.

names.name: Perez
names.gloss: A son of Judah and ancestor of David.

names.name: Ophel
names.gloss: The hill between the City of David and the Temple Mount.

names.name: Kiriath Arba
names.gloss: The old name for Hebron.

names.name: Beersheba
names.gloss: A town in the far south, traditionally the southern limit of the land.

names.name: valley of Hinnom
names.gloss: The valley south and west of Jerusalem.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: A priestly town north of Jerusalem, Jeremiah's home.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter lists families and towns. Read verses 1 and 2 on how Jerusalem was repopulated, then skim the rest.

insights.title: A tithe of people
insights.body: Jerusalem had walls but too few residents (7:4). The people cast lots so that one in ten would move to the city (11:1), a kind of tithe of the population. Living in the capital meant leaving family land and taking on the risks of a frontier town.

insights.title: Blessing the volunteers
insights.body: "The people blessed all the men who willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem" (11:2). Some went because the lot fell on them; others offered. The community honoured those who gave up their comfort for the city.

insights.title: The holy city
insights.body: Jerusalem is called "the holy city" (11:1, 11:18), a name that Isaiah uses and that Matthew and Revelation take up. Its holiness comes from God's presence in the Temple, not from its walls.

insights.title: From Beersheba to Hinnom
insights.body: The towns of Judah stretch from Beersheba in the south to the valley of Hinnom at Jerusalem (11:30). Several, such as Lachish, Azekah and Ziklag, appear in older stories. The list may describe where Jews lived or the land they claimed, since Persian Judah was smaller than the list suggests.

insights.title: Parallel in Chronicles
insights.body: A similar list of Jerusalem's residents appears in Chronicles, with differences in names and numbers. Both drew on community records kept after the return.

insights.title: Ordinary faithfulness
insights.body: After the drama of the wall and the covenant, the book turns to practicalities: who lives where, who guards the gates, who leads the singing. Rebuilding a community depends on such ordinary faithfulness as much as on great moments.

12.summary: After lists of priests and Levites across several generations, Jerusalem's wall is dedicated with two great choirs processing on the wall and joy heard far away.
12.lookfor: Skim the lists, then follow the two processions as they go round the wall in opposite directions and meet at the Temple.

names.name: Joiakim
names.gloss: High priest after his father Jeshua.

names.name: Jaddua
names.gloss: A high priest descended from Jeshua; the latest name in the book.

names.name: Darius the Persian
names.gloss: A Persian king, probably Darius II (423–404 BC).

names.name: Asaph
names.gloss: Chief singer in David's day, ancestor of the Temple musicians.

names.name: Netophathites
names.gloss: People of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.

names.name: Ezra the scribe
names.gloss: Leads one of the two processions.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 26 list priests and Levites from several generations. Skim them, then read the dedication of the wall from verse 27.

insights.title: Lists across a century
insights.body: The lists run from Jeshua's time to Jaddua's (12:10-11, 12:22), spanning several generations. They show the priesthood unbroken from the first return to the writer's own day. Josephus says a high priest Jaddua met Alexander the Great, though many scholars question his account.

insights.title: Two choirs on the wall
insights.body: Nehemiah set two great thanksgiving choirs on the wall (12:31). One went right toward the dung gate, the other left past the tower of the furnaces, and they met at the Temple (12:40). Marching on the wall itself showed it was solid, a reply to Tobiah's fox (4:3).

insights.title: Purifying the wall
insights.body: Before the dedication the priests and Levites purified themselves, the people, the gates and the wall (12:30). The walls themselves are treated as holy, marking Jerusalem as the holy city.

insights.title: Joy heard far away
insights.body: "The joy of Jerusalem was heard even far away" (12:43), and women and children joined in. At the founding of the Temple, joy had been mixed with weeping and the noise was heard far away. This time the note is pure joy.

insights.title: Dedication
insights.body: The word for "dedication" (12:27) is the Hebrew hanukkah, also used for the Temple's dedication and for the altar in the wilderness. The later Jewish feast of Hanukkah takes its name from the same word.

insights.title: As David commanded
insights.body: The music follows "the commandment of David the man of God" (12:24) with "the musical instruments of David" (12:36). The writer links worship after the exile to David's arrangements, showing continuity and keeping alive hopes connected with David's line.

insights.title: Celebrating finished work
insights.body: The people paused for a great public celebration before going back to ordinary life. How do you mark and give thanks for what God has helped you complete?

13.summary: Returning after a time away, Nehemiah finds the covenant broken: Tobiah lodged in the Temple, Levites unpaid, Sabbath trading, and mixed marriages, and he acts forcefully against each.
13.lookfor: Compare each problem with the promises in chapter 10, watch how Nehemiah responds each time, and notice how the book ends.

names.name: Balaam
names.gloss: A seer hired to curse Israel in the time of Moses.

names.name: Eliashib the priest
names.gloss: The priest in charge of the Temple storerooms, related by marriage to Tobiah.

names.name: Tobiah
names.gloss: The Ammonite official who had opposed the wall.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A Phoenician trading city on the coast, north of Israel.

names.name: Ashdod
names.gloss: A former Philistine city near the coast.

names.name: Sanballat the Horonite
names.gloss: Governor of Samaria and Nehemiah's old opponent.

insights.title: Ammonites and Moabites
insights.body: The law read aloud says no Ammonite or Moabite may enter God's assembly, because they hired Balaam to curse Israel (13:1-2). Deuteronomy gives the reason, adding that God "turned the curse into a blessing." Ruth the Moabite, David's ancestor, shows the Bible weighing this law alongside faith in Israel's God.

insights.title: What happened while he was away
insights.body: In Artaxerxes' thirty-second year, 433 BC, Nehemiah went back to the king (13:6). When he returned some time later, the reforms had slipped. Eliashib had given Tobiah a room in the Temple courts where the offerings were kept (13:5).

insights.title: Clearing out the Temple
insights.body: Nehemiah threw all of Tobiah's furniture out of the room (13:8) and had the rooms cleansed. Readers often compare Jesus driving the traders from the Temple courts. In both, zeal for God's house overturned what others had allowed.

insights.title: Why is God's house forsaken?
insights.body: The Levites had gone back to their fields because their share was not paid (13:10). Nehemiah asks, "Why is God's house forsaken?" (13:11), turning the people's own covenant words back on them. Malachi, likely a contemporary, raises the same complaint about tithes.

insights.title: Shutting the gates on the Sabbath
insights.body: Farmers brought produce into the city and Tyrian merchants sold fish on the Sabbath (13:15-16). Nehemiah had the gates shut from dusk before the Sabbath and threatened the traders camped outside (13:19-21). Jeremiah had warned against carrying burdens through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath.

insights.title: Half in the speech of Ashdod
insights.body: Children of mixed marriages spoke "half in the speech of Ashdod" and could not speak "the Jews' language" (13:24), meaning Hebrew. Losing the language meant losing access to the Scriptures and worship. Nehemiah's response, beating and pulling hair (13:25), is recorded without softening.

insights.title: The high priest's grandson
insights.body: One of the high priest's grandsons married Sanballat's daughter, and Nehemiah drove him away (13:28). Josephus tells a similar story of a priest named Manasseh who married Sanballat's daughter and became priest of a Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, though he dates it a century later.

insights.title: Remember me, my God
insights.body: The book ends with Nehemiah's prayer, "Remember me, my God, for good" (13:31). The ending is not triumphant: reforms keep slipping, and the community needs constant renewal. Many readers see in this the limits of reform and the need for a deeper change of heart promised by the prophets.

intro.who: Much of the book is Nehemiah's own first-person memoir, and Jewish tradition treats it with Ezra as one book written by Ezra and completed by Nehemiah. Most modern scholars see a later editor joining Nehemiah's memoir to lists, records and the account of Ezra reading the law.
intro.when: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, 445 BC, and returned for a second term after 433 BC. The book was probably put into its final form around 400 BC or somewhat later, since some lists run past Nehemiah's time.
intro.why: It tells how Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt and its people renewed their covenant with God, showing a small community regaining security, identity and faithfulness under Persian rule.
